text: A giant ring of wind above the North Pole just broke.
But this time, it broke earlier than ever recorded.
It's called the polar vortex. Think of a spinning fence that keeps freezing air locked over the Arctic.
On November tenth, those winds flipped. The earliest flip since records began in 1958, by almost three weeks.
So where does all that freezing air go? Wherever the jet stream bends.
After past breakdowns, parts of the eastern U.S., northern Europe and Asia usually turned colder the next month.
And it takes two to six weeks to reach the ground. That's right now... through December.
But it's not a promise. Some breakdowns barely change the weather.
So if your December gets brutal... blame the wind nineteen miles up.
